title: "Packages"
subtitle: "Checking, and fixing, which packages exist where your code runs"

## Introduction

::: {.answer}
"Installed" is a property of one R context, not of the cluster. Your session, the driver and each worker have their own library, so a package that loads in one says nothing about the others.
:::

That is why an install can appear not to have taken, and why the check below is worth running in each context rather than once. Start with the check, in your session and then in a worker, and then what to do when a package is missing from one.

## The check

Run this, and if it loads you are done. Most likely you are done.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
```
:::


Run it in the context you are asking about. That is the whole discipline of this page: a package that loads in your session tells you nothing about whether it loads in a worker, because those are different R installations with different library paths. To ask about a worker, ask inside one:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(sparklyr)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
check <- function(df) {
  pkgs <- c("sf", "terra", "dplyr")
  data.frame(
    pkg = pkgs,
    ok  = vapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
  )
}

tbl(sc, in_catalog(
  Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_CATALOG"),
  Sys.getenv("DATABRICKS_SCHEMA"),
  "hydrology_stations"
)) |>
  head(4) |>
  select(id = station_id) |>
  spark_apply(check, columns = "pkg string, ok boolean") |>
  collect()
```

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  pkg   ok   
  <chr> <lgl>
1 sf    TRUE 
2 terra TRUE 
3 dplyr TRUE 
```
:::


If they all come back `TRUE`, stop reading. The rest of this page is for the case where they do not.

Two checks, for the three contexts in the callout above, and the asymmetry is worth knowing. Your session and a worker are both places you can run R and ask directly. The driver is not, from a client connection: your session is the client, and the R that runs on the cluster runs inside the workers that `spark_apply()` starts. So the driver shows up here at install time rather than at check time, which is the trap in [What to send your admin](#what-to-send-your-admin) below: an install someone runs by hand touches the driver, and a worker never sees it.

## If it does not load

This is a workspace configuration matter, not something to fix from your session, and that is the fact worth having before you spend an afternoon on it.

For the geospatial stack the problem is usually not a missing R package at all. `install.packages("sf")` fails while configuring, because GDAL, GEOS and PROJ are absent from the runtime image. Those are system libraries, installed with root privileges on every machine in the cluster. You cannot install them from an R session, and no combination of `install.packages()` arguments changes that. Recognising this quickly is the point of the page: the error appears in R, so it reads as an R problem, and it is not one.

## What to send your admin

Forward [Setting up a cluster for geospatial R](../admin/geospatial-setup.qmd), which is written for them rather than for you, and say this much in your own words:

> The R geospatial packages need GDAL, GEOS and PROJ present on the cluster. `install.packages("sf")` fails at the configure step without them. They need to go in via an init script rather than an interactive install, because the script runs on every node and an interactive install only touches the driver.

That last sentence is the one worth keeping. An install that works when someone tries it by hand and then fails in a worker is the commonest way this gets misdiagnosed as fixed.

## Prebuilt library volumes

This is the good case, and it is worth being able to recognise it. Someone has already paid the build cost once, and left the result on a Unity Catalog volume:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.libPaths(c("/Volumes/your_catalog/your_schema/r_library", .libPaths()))
```
:::


The tree is reusable by any later cluster with the same R version and image, which is what makes it durable where an install is not. It works inside a worker too, which is what makes the geospatial parts of [Run a Monte Carlo simulation](../howdoi/monte-carlo.qmd) available to you at all.

Ask whether one exists before assuming it does not. It is a common enough arrangement that the answer is often yes.

## Why installs vanish

A package you upgraded may read as the old version next time you look, which looks exactly like the upgrade having failed.

It did not fail. Every R context gets its own library, and that library goes away. So the natural response, running the upgrade again, produces the same result and costs another afternoon.

The practical rule is to do everything that depends on an install in one context, in one session, without a break. If you need it to survive, that is the volume above, and it needs your administrator.

The version numbers themselves are worth checking rather than assuming: a worker can be on a different R patch release from your session, which matters if you ever compare hashes across the two. [Sending things to where your code runs](sending-things.qmd) covers that trap.

## Next

If a package is present but something else broke, [When it breaks](when-it-breaks.qmd) is organised by what you saw. Full setup detail, for whoever administers your workspace, is in [Setting up a cluster for geospatial R](../admin/geospatial-setup.qmd).
